newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures posted a small gain on Tuesday after a session driven largely by intra-day traders who bought in the morning and sold before the close as U.S. bonds declined, traders said.

They said there was little news fueling the early rally, besides a general impression that the 10-year part of the curve was in reasonable demand, and that the move was accentuated by a Bund rally and some buy-stops triggered after the open.
The slide into the close with U.S. bonds continued on GLOBEX and the contract hit support at 130.98 as traders carried on cutting positions put on today, traders said.
A trader at a U.S. house said "we're sitting on the sidelines, its mostly domestics, everything's under pressure with the U.S. (bond market)".
A trader at a large French bank said he was sceptical this morning's move had been sparked by short covering as he thought most shorts had been flushed out already.

He said the session was characterised by intra-day traders buying the contract in the morning, looking for some momentum, and then selling it in the afternoon. "That's what it looked like anyway," he said.
A trader at a French brokerage said the U.S. economic data released late in the session had a negative impact on the U.S. bond market and that had weighed on European bonds.
He said the contract looked set to trade within a fairly narrow range again on Wednesday with the area around 130.90 providing support and 131.44 likely to cap gains.
The spread between 10-year French and German yields remained unchanged at minus 12 basis points.
The spread between two and 10-year yields continued the narrowing trend seen during the past few days.
Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said the flattening had been driven from both ends of the curve by domestic and non-resident investors alike.
He said the recent slide in PIBOR contracts showed a rate rise in early 1998 was now being discounted and that the futures strip was dragging the cash bond market lower.

Longer-dated maturities were benefitting from the fact investors, who had been building up cash positions, had become more acclimatised to lower yields. Those reluctant to buy when 10-year yields first hit 5.50 percent were now comforted by the fact yields went on to fall as low as 5.30 percent, he said.

"When yields fell from six percent to 5.30 percent investors were digging in their heels. Now with yields above 5.55 percent the perspective has changed to the extent it's been demonstrated yields can go lower," he said. "They're now more happy to put their money to work."
Economists said they did not expect the Bank of France to cut the intervention rate from 3.10 percent after Thursday's monetary policy council meeting.
Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley, said he thought the French central bank would probably cut again but would prefer to wait for good inflation data in March and April.
The franc was slightly stronger against the mark at 3.3714 compared with 3.3725 late on Monday. Against the dollar it was at 5.7437 compared with a high of 5.7370 yesterday.
Call money was unchanged at 3-1/8 1/4 percent. It was last cut on January 31, the day after the intervention rate was trimmed five basis points to 3.10 percent.
The Treasury announced it would be offering 300 to 500 million Ecu of the 5.5 percent 2007 OAT at its regular auction on Thursday.
-- David Clarke, Paris Newsroom +331 4221 5452
